title: Measures of Central Tendency
outcomes: List the requisites of an ideal average and judge AM, median, mode, GM and HM against them.
Compute the AM (direct and step-deviation), median, mode, GM, HM and weighted averages for raw and grouped data.
Use the properties of averages — deviations, change of origin and scale, combined and corrected means, minimum absolute deviation.
Find quartiles, deciles and percentiles for raw and grouped data and read them from an ogive.
Apply the empirical relation Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean and the inequality AM ≥ GM ≥ HM (with AH = G² for two numbers).

meta.exam_tip: Central tendency is one of the highest-scoring areas of Part C. Expect 4–6 MCQs: combined/corrected mean, change of origin and scale, median/mode formula, empirical relation, AM–GM–HM. Learn the formulas so well that each takes under a minute.

concepts.title: Central tendency and the ideal average
body: A measure of central tendency (an average) is a single value around which the observations cluster and which represents the whole set. The five measures are arithmetic mean (AM), median (Me), mode (Mo), geometric mean (GM) and harmonic mean (HM).

An ideal measure should be (i) properly and unambiguously defined, (ii) easy to understand, (iii) simple to compute, (iv) based on all observations, (v) capable of mathematical treatment, and (vi) least affected by extreme observations (and by sampling fluctuations).
concepts.analogy: An average is a team captain — one person who represents everyone. A good captain is chosen by clear rules, understood by all, and not swayed by one loud member.
concepts.work: When a company reports "average realisation per tonne", analysts check which average was used. A mean dragged up by a few premium sales can mislead; that is why medians often appear in compensation disclosures.

concepts.title: Arithmetic mean and its properties
body: Raw data: x̄ = Σx/n. Grouped data: x̄ = Σfx/N with x the mid-value. Step-deviation (short-cut) method: take an origin A and class width C, d = (x − A)/C, then x̄ = A + (Σfd/N) × C.

Properties: (i) if every value is a constant k, the AM is k; (ii) the algebraic sum of deviations from the AM is zero — Σ(x − x̄) = 0, Σf(x − x̄) = 0; (iii) change of origin and scale: if y = a + bx then ȳ = a + b x̄; (iv) combined mean of two groups x̄ = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂), extendable to more groups.

Merits: rigidly defined, based on all values, easy, mathematically tractable, stable from sample to sample. Demerits: badly affected by extreme values and cannot be found for open-end classes without assuming mid-values.
concepts.analogy: The mean is the balancing point of a see-saw loaded with the observations — deviations on the two sides cancel exactly.
concepts.work: Correcting a mean after one wrong entry (subtract the wrong value, add the right one, divide again) is exactly how you fix an average debtor-days figure once a mis-keyed invoice is found.

concepts.title: Median
body: Median is the middle value when observations are arranged in order — half lie below it and half above. Raw data: the ((n + 1)/2)th value; for even n, the AM of the two middle values.

Grouped data: find N/2 in the less-than cumulative frequency column to locate the median class. Me = l₁ + ((N/2 − Nl)/(Nu − Nl)) × C, where l₁ = lower boundary of the median class, Nl and Nu = less-than c.f. at its lower and upper boundaries (Nu − Nl = its frequency) and C = its width. Graphically, it is the x-value where the two ogives meet (or where N/2 cuts the less-than ogive).
Properties: if y = a + bx, then median of y = a + b × median of x. The sum of absolute deviations Σ|x − A| is minimum when A is the median.
Merits: easy, not affected by extreme values, the best average for open-end classes. Demerits: not based on all observations and not amenable to algebraic treatment.
concepts.analogy: The median is the middle person in a queue sorted by height — the very tall basketball player at the end does not move him.
concepts.work: Median house price and median salary are quoted instead of means because a few very large values distort the mean.

concepts.title: Partition values — quartiles, deciles, percentiles
body: Quartiles split ordered data into 4 equal parts (Q₁, Q₂ = median, Q₃); deciles into 10 parts (D₁ … D₉); percentiles into 100 parts (P₁ … P₉₉). Hence Q₂ = D₅ = P₅₀ = median, and Q₁ = P₂₅, Q₃ = P₇₅.

Raw data (ICAI rule): Q₁ is the ((n + 1)/4)th value, Q₃ the (3(n + 1)/4)th, Dₖ the (k(n + 1)/10)th, Pₖ the (k(n + 1)/100)th. For a fractional position, interpolate: 2.75th value = 2nd value + 0.75 × (3rd − 2nd).
Grouped data: replace N/2 in the median formula by Np (N/4 for Q₁, 3N/4 for Q₃, kN/10 for Dₖ …). Graphically, draw a horizontal line at Np to the less-than ogive and drop a perpendicular.
concepts.analogy: Cutting a sorted loaf into 4, 10 or 100 equal slices — the cut positions are the quartiles, deciles and percentiles.
concepts.work: "Top-quartile" fund performance, "90th percentile" response times in service contracts and salary benchmarking bands are all partition values.

concepts.title: Mode and the empirical relationship
body: Mode is the value that occurs most often. It may not exist (all values occur equally often) or there may be more than one (bimodal).

Grouped data: the modal class has the highest frequency. Mo = l₁ + ((f₀ − f₋₁)/(2f₀ − f₋₁ − f₁)) × C, where f₀, f₋₁, f₁ are the frequencies of the modal, pre-modal and post-modal classes. Graphically, the mode is found from the histogram.
Empirical relation (moderately skewed distributions): Mean − Mode = 3(Mean − Median), i.e. Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean. Also, if y = a + bx, the mode of y = a + b × mode of x.

Merits: easy, the most "typical" value, not affected by extremes, usable for qualitative data. Demerits: may be undefined or multiple, has no mathematical properties and is affected by sampling fluctuations.
concepts.analogy: The mode is the most popular dish at a canteen — the one ordered most, not the "average" dish.
concepts.work: Retailers stock to the modal size; quality teams look at the modal defect type first.

concepts.title: Geometric mean and harmonic mean
body: GM of n positive values = (x₁ × x₂ × … × xₙ)^(1/n); log G = (Σ log x)/n — the log of the GM is the AM of the logs. Grouped: log G = Σf log x / N.
Properties of GM: if all values are k, GM = k; GM of a product z = xy is GM(x) × GM(y); GM of a ratio z = x/y is GM(x) ÷ GM(y). Use: average rates of growth, ratios, percentages and index numbers.

HM = n / Σ(1/x); grouped: N / Σ(f/x). If all values are k, HM = k. Combined HM of two groups = (n₁ + n₂)/(n₁/H₁ + n₂/H₂). Use: average of rates (speed, price per unit) when the distance or money spent is the same for each rate.
GM and HM are rigidly defined and based on all observations, but harder to understand and compute, so their use is limited to rates and ratios.

concepts.analogy: GM is the "compound interest" average; HM is the "same-distance" average.
concepts.work: CAGR quoted in equity research is a GM. The average cost per unit when a fixed amount is invested every month (rupee-cost averaging) is an HM of the prices.

concepts.title: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM, weighted averages and choosing an average
body: For positive observations AM ≥ GM ≥ HM; equality holds only when all observations are equal. For two positive numbers a and b: A = (a + b)/2, G = √(ab), H = 2ab/(a + b), and A × H = G². This identity holds only for two numbers.
Weighted averages: weighted AM = Σwx/Σw; weighted GM = antilog(Σw log x/Σw); weighted HM = Σw/Σ(w/x). Use when observations differ in importance (marks with credit weights, prices with quantities).

Choosing: AM is usually the best (rigid, all values, stable) but avoid it with extreme values or open-end classes; median for open-end classes and skewed data; mode for the most typical value or qualitative data; GM for growth rates and ratios; HM for rates with a fixed numerator.
concepts.analogy: Three cousins who always stand in the same order of height — AM tallest, HM shortest — unless everyone in the family is identical.
concepts.work: A cost accountant averaging material rates weights each rate by quantity (weighted AM). An investment analyst averaging P/E ratios across a portfolio of equal investments may use an HM.

jobs.title: Which "average" goes into the board note?
jobs.role: Management accountant in a retail chain
jobs.situation: Average bill value across 50,000 bills is ₹1,240, but 300 corporate bulk bills above ₹50,000 pull it up. The median bill is ₹640 and the most common bill band is ₹400–500.
steps: Explain that the mean is distorted by a few extreme bills — it does not describe a typical customer.
Report the median (₹640) as the typical bill and the modal band for store staffing and stocking.
Keep the mean for revenue planning, because total revenue = mean × number of bills.
Show quartiles (Q₁, Q₃) so the board sees the spread of the middle 50% of bills.
jobs.takeaway: Choose the average that answers the question: totals → mean; typical value → median; most common → mode.
jobs.think: Which average still lets you recover total revenue?
jobs.answer: Only the arithmetic mean: total = mean × count.

jobs.title: Computing CAGR for an equity research note
jobs.role: Research associate at a broking house
jobs.situation: A company's revenue was ₹500 crore and is ₹845 crore four years later after uneven growth each year.
steps: Average growth of a compounding quantity needs the GM of growth factors, not the AM of percentages.
Cross-check by compounding ₹500 crore at 14.02% for four years.
State the base and end year clearly — CAGR is sensitive to the choice of endpoints.
jobs.takeaway: CAGR is a geometric mean; an AM of yearly growth rates always overstates it when rates vary.

viva.q: State the important properties of the arithmetic mean.
viva.model: If all observations equal a constant, the mean is that constant. The algebraic sum of deviations of the observations from their mean is zero. The mean is affected by change of origin and scale: if y equals a plus b x, the mean of y is a plus b times the mean of x. And two groups can be combined: the combined mean is n1 x1 bar plus n2 x2 bar divided by n1 plus n2.

viva.q: Why is the median preferred for open-ended distributions, and what is its minimum property?
viva.model: The median is a positional average; it needs only the cumulative frequencies up to the middle, so open-end classes do not matter, and it is not affected by extreme values. Its special property is that the total of the absolute deviations is least when they are measured from the median.

viva.q: What is the relationship between AM, GM and HM? What special result holds for two positive numbers?
viva.model: For positive observations, the arithmetic mean is greater than or equal to the geometric mean, which is greater than or equal to the harmonic mean; they are equal only when all observations are equal. For two positive numbers, AM multiplied by HM equals the square of GM.

viva.q: When should we use the geometric mean and when the harmonic mean?
viva.model: The geometric mean is used to average rates of growth, ratios and percentage changes, for example average annual growth of sales or in index numbers, because the changes compound. The harmonic mean is used to average rates such as speed or price per unit when the distance or the amount spent is fixed, for example the average speed over equal distances.

cases.title: Salary analysis for an HR policy note
cases.case: Tanvi, a CA in a mid-sized firm, is asked to report "average" salaries. The firm has three departments: Audit (12 staff, mean ₹38,000), Tax (30 staff, mean ₹24,000) and Advisory (18 staff, mean ₹29,000). The salary register is grouped with an open last class "₹60,000 and above". Revenue grew by 8%, 15% and 25% in the last three years. One partner wants the "most common" salary band highlighted.

mcqs.q: What is the combined mean salary of the 60 staff?
mcqs.explain: Combined mean = (12 × 38,000 + 30 × 24,000 + 18 × 29,000) ÷ 60 = ₹28,300. ₹30,333 is the simple average of the three means — wrong, because group sizes differ.

mcqs.q: With an open-ended last class, which average can be computed from the grouped register without assuming a mid-value?
mcqs.explain: The median needs only cumulative frequencies up to the middle; AM, GM and HM need every class mid-value, which the open class lacks.

mcqs.q: The average annual revenue growth over the three years is closest to:
mcqs.explain: Growth compounds, so use the GM of growth factors: (1.08 × 1.15 × 1.25)^(1/3) − 1 = 1.5525^(1/3) − 1 ≈ 15.79%. The AM of 8, 15 and 25 (16%) overstates it; 55.25% is the total growth over three years.

mcqs.q: The "most common salary band" requested by the partner is the:
mcqs.explain: Mode is the value (or class) with the highest frequency — the most common one.
